<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Ayanna Pressley, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Sean Casten, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: There is limited discussion of either illicit finance
or cybersecurity in the Clarity Act--many more pages
are honed on establishing large regulatory carve-outs
than on establishing expectations, driving needed
industry standards or sponsoring research and
development, or appropriating necessary resources to
ensure appropriately scaled and timely enforcement of
these critical requirements. Also important to note,
especially in light of recent changes in enforcement
posture--beyond just creating the policy framework, the
government and industry must work to apply and enforce
the framework. A policy that isn't enforced or
implemented does nothing to benefit consumers nor U.S.
firms . . .\40\
\40\House Committee on Financial Services, Testimony of Carole House, Democratic Minority Day: Continuation of American Innovation and the Future of Digital Assets: From Blueprint to a Functional Framework, 119th Cong. (June 6, 2025).
The CALAMITY Act does say that the new category of entities would be ``financial institutions'' (FIs) for the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), but that is simply stating the status quo: these entities are already regulated under the BSA as FIs. Democrats pointed out that there are many FIs under the BSA that have little or no compliance requirements, thus adding specificity to ensure that they're expected to comply at least to the same level as other FIs under the CFTC would be warranted (i.e., at a higher level than they are currently regulated), yet that was rejected. Given the criminal activity facilitated by digital assets,\41\ (such as ransomware, pig butchering, investment scams, etc.), as crypto adoption increases, so will the prevalence of those crimes; unfortunately, Republicans also rejected any provisions that would bolster related transparency, guidance, investigations, and even victim support, and thus, these obvious threat vectors are effectively ignored. Section 110 of the CALAMITY Act prevents blockchain developers and other providers from being classified as ``money transmitters'' thus stopping any application of the BSA\56\ among other laws and regulations. This includes not only individual software developers, but also companies that are already supporting billions of dollars in crypto activity each year, using ``defi'' applications on the blockchain. Along with the bill's broad exemption for the entirety of the decentralized finance (DeFi) industry, found in Sections 309 and 409, this is alarming.\42\ In addition to affecting the application of economic and trade sanctions, it could prevent tax, consumer protection, disclosure, whistleblower, anti-corruption and other laws or regulations from applying. It is effectively a permanent safe harbor allowing them to avoid liabilities from future law or regulation, no matter how the blockchain and blockchain services change.
\41\U.S. Secret Service, Combating the Illicit Use of Digital Assets (accessed June 8, 2025).
\42\Number Analytics, S. Lee, 10 Revolutionary Stats on DeFi Applications in 2023 Market (Mar. 25, 2025).
STATE PREEMPTION
This legislation also takes the state securities regulators off the frontlines of fighting fraud. The CALAMITY Act is silent on whether state securities regulators have antifraud, investigation, and examination authorities, as well as the authority to regulate the brokerage and investment advisory industries.
At best, states would be forced to spend enormous resources litigating and proving in courts that the states still have these authorities to help prevent and fight fraud.\43\ The CALAMITY Act's silence could also result in multiple de facto regulatory gaps that foster fraud and leave victims without recourse. For example, the U.S. federal government almost never takes on cases where the harmed investor's losses are small. By contrast, state securities regulators regularly pursue cases under $1 million to help the victim recover what may amount to their entire lifesavings.
\43\See, CRS ``Federal Preemption: A Legal Primer.''
ANTICOMPETITIVE BUSINESS PRACTICES
Anticompetitive business practices restrict competition in the market and can lead to monopolies or dominant firms that leave smaller businesses with high barriers to entry. This bill bakes in the harmful practices by dominant crypto firms, allowing them to consolidate power within one company, known as vertical integration. The CALAMITY Act would allow the same entity, and affiliates it controls, to comingle the following functions, that are separate under today's securities laws to avoid clear conflicts of interest: running an exchange facility; operating an alternative trading system; conducting broker-dealer activity; settling and clearing trades; custodying assets; and offering wallet services. This legislation also does not include best execution requirements, which require brokers to carry out customer orders under the most favorable conditions to customers.\44\ Under this bill, exchanges would also not have to post the National Best Bid or Offer (NBBO), which is a stock quote available market wide that represents the highest buy price and the lowest sell price for a security trading on various exchanges.\45\ The NBBO was created by the SEC to ensure customers get the best available price at the time of a trade, no matter where they execute their trade.\46\
\44\Best Execution Rule: What it is, Requirements and FAQ, Investopedia (Mar. 18, 2024).
\45\NBBO: What It Is and How It's Calculated, SoFi Learn (Sept. 1, 2023).
\46\NBBO: What It Is and How It's Calculated, SoFi Learn (Sept. 1, 2023).
Additionally, the biggest traditional finance entities, including the big banks, will be empowered by the complexities of this bill because they will be the best equipped to game the loopholes created by this bill and ensure all of their activity comes under the light touch regulation the bill provides. This means less investment for crypto entrepreneurs. This bill would also codify the dominance of the largest crypto firms, at the expense of startups in the space.
Democrats offered over 27 amendments aimed at addressing the deficiencies with the CALAMITY Act, all of which were rejected by Republicans or withdrawn:\47\
\47\House Committee on Financial Services, Committee Markup, 119th Cong. (June 10, 2025).
• The Ranking Member's amendment (#1) adds the
``Stop TRUMP in Crypto Act'', which blocks the
President, Vice President, Members of Congress, and
their immediate families from engaging crypto
corruption and blatant conflicts of interest.
• Rep. Casten's amendment (#1) would prohibit
the SEC and CFTC from finalizing joint rulemakings
required under the bill unless the agencies can meet
quorum (i.e., 3 confirmed commissioners) and there is
representation from both political parties.
• The Ranking Member's amendment (#3)
establishes a crypto investors and consumers bill of
rights.
• The Ranking Member's amendment (#2) ensures
states maintain power to address fraud in the crypto
industry.
• Rep. Sherman's amendment (#1) prevents
federal bailouts if a stablecoin or crypto issuer fails
or goes bankrupt.
• Rep. Sherman's amendment (#2) prevents the
federal government and the Federal Reserve Banks from
purchasing crypto and Trump from enriching himself
through the crypto strategic reserve.
• Rep. Sherman's amendment (#3) bans digital
assets from being used in campaign contributions.
• Rep. Sherman's amendment (#4) ensures
wallets comply with Anti-Money Laundering requirements,
including Know Your Customer rules.
• Rep. Lynch's amendment (#2) reconstitutes
the Department of Justice's National Cryptocurrency
Enforcement Team and calls on them to investigate
Trump's crypto companies.
• Rep. Foster's amendment (#2) requires the
SEC and CFTC to establish a Senior Scam Hotline to
provide assistance to older Americans in avoiding
fraud, scams, and other abuse related to digital
assets. This amendment would also require all Bitcoin
ATMs to clearly display information about the Senior
Scam Hotline on the Bitcoin ATM.
• Rep. Garcia's amendment (#1) ensures parity
with traditional financial institutions under the Bank
Secrecy Act. It creates a clear, enforceable obligation
for custodians to monitor and report illicit financing.
This approach helps to bridge the gap that the bill
provides by bringing cross-border digital asset flows
back under the same scrutiny that the traditional
banking system must adhere to.
• Rep. Pressley's amendment requires that the
U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) conduct a
study on the financial abuse and exploitation of
vulnerable populations, including elderly individuals
and individuals who are victims of domestic violence.
• Rep Casten's amendment (#2) directs the
Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network
(FinCEN) to finalize its rule on cryptocurrency mixers
within one year of enactment of the CALAMITY Act. A
mixer is an anonymity enhancing service that obfuscates
transactional information that would otherwise be
visible on a public blockchain. For example, while
transactions under a traditional financial system are
private by default, most digital assets operate on
public blockchains and can, therefore, be seen by
anyone.\48\
\48\FinCEN, FinCEN Proposes New Regulation to Enhance Transparency in Convertible Virtual Currency Mixing and Combat Terrorist Financing (Oct. 19, 2023); What is a cryptocurrency mixer and how does it work?, CoinTelegraph (May 27, 2025).
• Rep. Tlaib's amendment prohibits crypto
issued by a company owned, affiliated, or controlled by
the President or their family members from being
required to be used to conduct transactions with the
government.
• Rep. Lynch's amendment (#1) requires the
Inspector Generals of the Treasury and the SEC to
conduct an annual report on any presidential crypto
holdings.
• Rep. Lynch's amendment (#2) amends the
Patriot Act and permits financial institutions to share
information about cyber-enabled financial crime and
fraud. This would allow financial institutions to
identify and report to the federal government
activities that may involve money laundering or
terrorist activities.
• Rep. Lynch's amendment (#4) strikes language
in the bill that adds innovation to the Securities and
Exchange Commission's mission. Adding an innovation
mandate is unnecessary because the SEC's long-held
mission to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly
and efficient markets and facilitate capital formation
already has innovation built in.
• Rep. Himes amendment (#1) prohibits
federally elected officials from issuing any digital
assets or owning a financial stake in an issuer.
• Rep. Himes' amendment (#2) strikes the
provision which creates a new exemption for crypto
issuers to raise capital from retail investors without
needing to provide them with reliable financial
disclosures or even requiring the proceeds to be used
to develop the blockchain project.
• Rep. Himes' amendment (#3) this amendment
would strike a paragraph in Section 205 of the bill,
the unworkable review process by the SEC to determine
the maturity of a blockchain. This amendment would then
authorize the SEC to receive the necessary information
to determine whether a blockchain is mature.
• Rep. Foster's amendment (#3) establishes a
joint Financial Influencer Task Force between the SEC
and CFTC to consult with the Federal Trade Commission,
financial influencers, and social media firms to
oversee online financial advice, track complaints,
educate investors, and coordinate global standards.
• Rep. Garcia's amendment (#2) ensures
blockchain systems follow the same recordkeeping rules
as traditional systems, supporting the Bank Secrecy
Act's Travel Rule, with basic standards for collecting
and keeping records.
• Rep. Fields' amendment requires any trading
platform offering digital commodities or related
investment contracts to provide users with educational
materials that are approved by the SEC.
